chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, from Ja'far, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), that Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) heard a man saying:
"A greedy person is more treacherous than an unjust person."
He (the Imam) said to him, "You are mistaken. An unjust person may repent, seek forgiveness, and return the usurped property to its owners."
But a greedy person, when he exercises greed, withholds Zakat, charity, maintaining kinship ties, hosting guests, spending in the way of Allah, and the gates of virtue."
And it is forbidden for Paradise to admit a greedy person.
ai.seo_question: Why is a greedy person considered more treacherous than an unjust person in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates that Amir al-Mu'minin Ali (peace be upon him) refutes the notion that stinginess is worse than injustice by highlighting the comprehensive nature of a miser's deprivation. While an unjust person may repent and restore specific rights, the stingy person systematically withholds Zakat, Sadaqah, Silat al-Rahim (kinship ties), and hospitality, effectively closing all 'doors of goodness.' This cumulative withholding renders Paradise forbidden to them, a concept deeply rooted in Shia ethical teachings on social responsibility.
